label: W4·1
title: Quiz 1 walkthrough: what each version asked and how to answer
hook: After this lesson you can answer any version of Quiz 1 (draw the methodology + find ROI, BEP and NPV), because the midterm will very likely ask the same kind of thing.

cards.body:
The professor gave Quiz 1 at the start of the W4 lecture. It did not test W4. It tested the two lectures before it: W1b (methodology pictures) and W3 (money calculations).

There were 4 versions. Each one had 2 open tasks and no answer options:

  1. Part A: "Depict graphically: ___ development methodology." You draw a W1b picture from memory.
  2. Part B: a list of cash flows, then "Find: ROI, BEP and NPV, if project life cycle is 3 years and rate of return = X%".

The versions are almost the same. Only 3 amounts and the rate change. So he tests the method, not memorised numbers. Learn the method once and you can do every version.

cards.h: The four versions side by side
cards.body:
The same in every version: Office space and equipment 40,000 and Vendor installation 50,000 (development); Software upgrades 20,000 and Operational team salaries 10,000 (operational); Reduction in staff 40,000 and Better supplier prices 30,000 (benefits); life cycle 3 years.

V1 (S2)V2 (S3)V3 (S4)V4 (S5)
Part A: drawPhasedWaterfallParallelPhased
Data conversion tools (dev.)10,00020,00030,00040,000
User training (oper.)20,00010,00010,00010,000
Increased sales (benefit)20,00040,00060,00080,000
Rate of return5%10%15%20%

Notice: Phased was asked twice (V1 and V4). Be very ready to draw it.

cards.h: Part A: the drawing rules, and Waterfall (V2)
cards.body:
The full drawing lessons are in the W1b methodology lessons. Here is the quick version.

Rules the professor's pictures always follow:

  • one box per phase (Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation);
  • a solid arrow forward to the next phase;
  • a dashed wavy arrow back to the previous phase;
  • a rounded box for the output ("System", "System version 1");
  • a dotted ellipse around a group that repeats or runs on its own ("Subproject 1").

Waterfall = a staircase going down: Planning → Analysis → Design → Implementation → System. Add 2–3 lines: "plan-driven; each phase finishes before the next starts; going back is hard and costly."
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  P[Planning] --> A[Analysis]
  A --> D[Design]
  D --> I[Implementation]
  I --> S([System])
  A -.->|back| P
  D -.->|back| A
  I -.->|back| D

cards.body:
Idea: build the system in versions, one after another. Version 1 has the most important requirements. Users try it, and what they learn goes into version 2.

Draw: Planning and Analysis once. Then several small cycles (Analysis → Design → Implementation), each inside a dotted ellipse, each ending in a rounded "System version n". A long arrow goes from each version into the Analysis of the next cycle.

Pro: a useful system reaches users quickly. Con: users work with a system that is "intentionally incomplete". It is a RAD methodology.

flowchart TD
  P[Planning] --> A0[Analysis]
  subgraph C1["Version 1 cycle"]
    direction LR
    A1[Analysis] --> D1[Design] --> I1[Implementation]
  end
  I1 --> S1(["System version 1"])
  S1 --> A2

cards.body:
Idea: do one general design for the whole system, then split the work into subprojects that are designed and built at the same time. At the end the pieces are integrated into one system.

Draw: Planning → Analysis → Design, then 3 dotted ellipses "Subproject 1/2/3" (each Design → Implementation), all joining into Integration → System.

Pro: "can reduce the time to deliver a system". Con: the system still comes only at the end, like waterfall. It is a Structured methodology (not RAD).

cards.h: Part B: the 6-step money recipe (from W3)
cards.body:
1. Classify. Development costs happen once, in Year 0. Operational costs and tangible benefits happen every year (Years 1, 2, 3). Write this assumption on your paper.
  2. Table. Columns Year 0 … Year 3 and Total. Rows: Total Benefits, Total Costs, Net Benefits (= B − C), Cumulative. (Parentheses) = negative.
  3. ROI = (Total Benefits − Total Costs) / Total Costs, using the Total column (Year 0 included).
  4. BEP. Find the first year the cumulative becomes positive ("that year"). BEP = (number of negative years, not counting Year 0) + (that year's net − that year's cumulative) / that year's net.
  5. PV = amount / (1 + r)n. Year 0 is not discounted.
  6. NPV = sum of PV of benefits − sum of PV of costs. NPV > 0 → "economically acceptable".

Classic mistakes: putting User training or Software upgrades in Year 0 (they are operational); discounting Year 0; counting Year 0 as a negative year in BEP.

VersionDev (Y0)Oper/yrBenefits/yrNet/yrROIBEPNPV
V1, 5%100,00050,00090,00040,0008.00%2.50 yrs$8,929.92
V2, 10%110,00040,000110,00070,00043.48%1.57 yrs$64,079.64
V3, 15%120,00040,000130,00090,00062.50%1.33 yrs$85,490.26
V4, 20%130,00040,000150,000110,00080.00%1.18 yrs$101,712.96

All four NPVs are positive, so all four projects are economically acceptable. V1 is the "tight" one: at 10% instead of 5% its NPV would turn negative.

Fast check (only when the yearly net is the same every year): NPV = −Dev + Net × (sum of the 3 discount factors). For V2: −110,000 + 70,000 × 2.48685 = 64,079.64 ✓. On the exam still show the full table.

example.problem: Quiz 1, Version 1 (S2). Development: Office space and equipment $40,000; Vendor installation $50,000; Data conversion tools $10,000. Operational: Software upgrades $20,000; Operational team salaries $10,000; User training $20,000. Tangible benefits: Increased sales $20,000; Reduction in staff $40,000; Better supplier prices $30,000. Find ROI, BEP and NPV, life cycle 3 years, rate of return 5%.
example.solution:
Assumption: development costs are one-time in Year 0; operational costs and benefits repeat every year, Years 1–3, with no growth.

Step 1, classify and add: Development = 40,000 + 50,000 + 10,000 = 100,000 (Year 0). Operational = 20,000 + 10,000 + 20,000 = 50,000 per year. Benefits = 20,000 + 40,000 + 30,000 = 90,000 per year.

Step 2, the table:

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3Total
Total Benefits090,00090,00090,000270,000
Total Costs100,00050,00050,00050,000250,000
Net Benefits(100,000)40,00040,00040,00020,000
Cumulative(100,000)(60,000)(20,000)20,000
Divide by 1.05n11.051.10251.157625
PV of Benefits085,714.2981,632.6577,745.38245,092.32
PV of Costs100,000.0047,619.0545,351.4743,191.88236,162.40

ROI = (270,000 − 250,000) / 250,000 = 20,000 / 250,000 = 8.00%

BEP: the cumulative first becomes positive in Year 3. Negative years before it (not counting Year 0): Years 1 and 2 = 2. BEP = 2 + (40,000 − 20,000) / 40,000 = 2 + 0.5 = 2.50 years.

NPV = 245,092.32 − 236,162.40 = $8,929.92 > 0 → the project is economically acceptable.

check.q: Which two lectures did Quiz 1 test?
check.a: W1b (methodology diagrams) and W3 (economic feasibility: ROI, BEP, NPV). Not the W4 topic of that day.

check.q: In which year do you put 'User training' and 'Software upgrades'?
check.a: Every year, Years 1–3. They are operational costs, not development costs.

check.q: Do you discount the Year 0 development cost when you compute PV?
check.a: No. Year 0 money is already 'today's money', so it stays the same: (1 + r)0 = 1. Year 0 is not discounted.

check.q: In V2 the cumulative is (40,000) in Year 1 and 30,000 in Year 2, net 70,000 per year. What is the BEP?
Which methodology was asked in two versions, and is it Structured or RAD?
check.a: Phased development (V1 and V4). It is a RAD methodology. Parallel and Waterfall are Structured.

exam.question: (Quiz 1, Version 3, S4.) (a) Depict graphically: Parallel development methodology. (b) Development: Office space and equipment $40,000; Vendor installation $50,000; Data conversion tools $30,000. Operational: Software upgrades $20,000; Operational team salaries $10,000; User training $10,000. Tangible benefits: Increased sales $60,000; Reduction in staff $40,000; Better supplier prices $30,000. Find ROI, BEP and NPV, if project life cycle is 3 years and rate of return = 15%.
exam.answer:
(a) Draw the picture below: one general design, then 3 subprojects (Design → Implementation, in dotted ellipses) running in parallel, then Integration → System. Add wavy back-arrows between boxes. Write: "General design for the whole system, then subprojects designed and implemented in parallel, then integrated. Pro: shorter time to deliver. Con: system delivered only at the end."

(b) Assumption: development costs in Year 0; operational costs and benefits every year, Years 1–3.

Development = 40,000 + 50,000 + 30,000 = 120,000. Operational = 20,000 + 10,000 + 10,000 = 40,000/yr. Benefits = 60,000 + 40,000 + 30,000 = 130,000/yr.

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3Total
Total Benefits0130,000130,000130,000390,000
Total Costs120,00040,00040,00040,000240,000
Net Benefits(120,000)90,00090,00090,000150,000
Cumulative(120,000)(30,000)60,000150,000
PV of Benefits (÷1.15n)0113,043.4898,298.6885,477.11296,819.27
PV of Costs120,000.0034,782.6130,245.7526,300.65211,329.00

ROI = 150,000 / 240,000 = 62.50%. BEP = 1 + (90,000 − 60,000) / 90,000 = 1.33 years. NPV = 296,819.27 − 211,329.00 = $85,490.26 > 0 → economically acceptable.

V1 Phased 5% · V2 Waterfall 10% · V3 Parallel 15% · V4 Phased 20%

ROI = (B − C) / C on totals; BEP: don't count Year 0; NPV: don't discount Year 0

label: W4·2
title: Choosing projects and running them: classify, select, 5 stages, tasks
hook: After this lesson you can define project management, list the 7 ways to classify a project, the 4 selection steps, the 5 process stages, and what information describes one task.

cards.body:
Think of the IT department of a big university. Everyone wants a new system: course registration, a library app, a dorm portal. There are more requests than people and money.

The slide says exactly this: demand for IT projects "far exceeds" what the department can supply. The CIO must choose projects with the highest return while managing risk. One study (AMR Research) found 2–15% of IT projects are not even strategic. So the department must prioritize, select and manage its portfolio of projects.

Project management = "the process of planning and controlling the project within a specified time frame, at minimum cost, with the desired outcomes". The project manager coordinates hundreds of tasks. It is a real profession: the PMP certificate from the Project Management Institute (PMI).

Where we are (S6): in the Planning phase, W3 finished the first half (system request + feasibility). W4 starts the second half: estimate time, identify tasks, WBS, PERT and Gantt charts, manage scope, assess risk.

WayThe question it asks
SizeHow many people are needed?
CostHow much will it cost the organization?
PurposeImprove the technical infrastructure? Support a current business strategy? Improve operations? Demonstrate a new innovation?
LengthHow long until it is finished, and until value reaches the business?
RiskHow likely is it to succeed or fail?
ScopeHow much of the organization is affected: a department, a division, the whole corporation?
Return on investmentHow much money comes back for what it costs?

Memory aid: "Some Cats Purr Loudly, Rarely Scratching Owners" = Size, Cost, Purpose, Length, Risk, Scope, ROI.

The slide is a picture of 4 circles, left to right. It gives no details, just the names:

  1. Identify potential projects
  2. Compare the projects
  3. Analyze your findings
  4. Select a project

Link: in step 2 you compare projects using the 7 classification questions (cost, risk, ROI…). Memory aid: I-C-A-S.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A["1. Identify potential projects"] --> B["2. Compare the projects"]
  B --> C["3. Analyze your findings"]
  C --> D["4. Select a project"]

cards.h: The 5 stages of the project management process (S10)
cards.body:
StageWhat happens
1. InitiationDefine purpose, scope, objectives; identify key stakeholders; create the project charter
2. PlanningCreate the project plan; create the WBS; develop a risk management strategy
3. ExecutionStart working; build workflows; assign tasks; keep everyone in the loop
4. Monitoring & ControllingRegular reviews; monitor progress against KPIs; apply changes when needed
5. ClosureComplete deliverables; discuss failures and successes; document lessons learned

Exam trap: the WBS and the risk strategy belong to stage 2, Planning. The charter belongs to stage 1, Initiation.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR
  I([Initiation]) --> P([Planning]) --> E([Execution]) --> M(["Monitoring and Controlling"]) --> C([Closure])
  M -.->|changes| E

cards.h: The 3 tools, and what a task is (S11–S13)
cards.body:
The 3 traditional project management tools: a work breakdown structure (WBS), a Gantt chart, and a network diagram (PERT and CPM). They help you list all tasks, their order, and how long each takes. (Next lesson teaches all three.)

A task = "a unit of work that will be performed by a member or members of the development team, such as feasibility analysis". The slide describes a task with 10 pieces of information:

InformationSlide example
NamePerform economic feasibility
Start date / Completion dateJan 05 / Jan 19, 2010
Person assignedProject sponsor: Mary Smith
Deliverable(s)Cost–benefit analysis
Completion statusOpen
PriorityHigh
Resources neededSpreadsheet software
Estimated time / Actual time16 hours / 14.5 hours

example.problem: A Tashkent café chain wants an online ordering app for its 12 cafés. 5 developers, $60,000, about 6 months. It should raise sales. Classify this project using the 7 ways from S8.
example.solution:
• Size: small/medium team, 5 people.
  • Cost: $60,000.
  • Purpose: support a business strategy (more online sales) and improve operations.
  • Length: about 6 months; value comes when the app goes live.
  • Risk: moderate (new technology for the staff, customers must adopt the app).
  • Scope: the whole company (all 12 cafés), not one department.
  • ROI: compare the extra sales with the $60,000 (the W3 method).

check.q: Give the slide's definition of project management.
check.a: The process of planning and controlling the project within a specified time frame, at minimum cost, with the desired outcomes.

check.q: List the 7 ways to classify projects.
check.a: Size, Cost, Purpose, Length, Risk, Scope, Return on investment.

check.q: In which stage of the PM process do you create the WBS? And the project charter?
check.a: WBS: stage 2, Planning. Project charter: stage 1, Initiation.

check.q: What are the 3 traditional project management tools?
check.a: Work breakdown structure, Gantt chart, network diagram.

check.q: In the S13 example, was the task finished faster or slower than estimated?
check.a: Faster: estimated 16 hours, actual 14.5 hours (1.5 hours under).

exam.question: Name and briefly describe the five stages of the project management process.
exam.answer:
1. Initiation: define purpose, scope and objectives, find key stakeholders, create the project charter.
  2. Planning: make the project plan, the work breakdown structure and a risk management strategy.
  3. Execution: start the work, build workflows, assign tasks, keep everyone informed.
  4. Monitoring and controlling: regular reviews, check progress against KPIs, apply changes.
  5. Closure: complete the deliverables, discuss failures and successes, document lessons learned.

memorize: PM = planning and controlling within a time frame, at minimum cost, with desired outcomes
7 ways: Size, Cost, Purpose, Length, Risk, Scope, ROI
Select: Identify → Compare → Analyze → Select
5 stages: Initiation → Planning → Execution → Monitoring & Controlling → Closure
3 tools: WBS, Gantt chart, network diagram
Task = a unit of work done by team member(s)

label: W4·3
title: WBS → Gantt chart → network diagram → critical path
hook: After this lesson you can build a WBS, draw a Gantt chart and a network diagram, compute PERT estimates, and find the critical path and the total project duration with a forward pass.

cards.h: The big chain: from tasks to pictures
cards.body:
Imagine you organise a wedding. First you write down every job and how long it takes. Then you group the jobs. Then you draw them on a calendar so everyone sees the plan.

A project manager does the same (S14):

  1. Identify the tasks and how long each one takes.
  2. Organise them in a work breakdown structure (WBS).
  3. The WBS drives two pictures: the Gantt chart and the network diagram.
  4. Use the pictures to manage progress over time.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR
  T["Identify tasks and durations"] --> W["WBS: numbered list"]
  W --> G["Gantt chart: bars on a calendar"]
  W --> N["Network diagram: boxes and arrows"]
  N --> C["CPM: critical path"]

cards.body:
A WBS is "a list of tasks hierarchically numbered". You build it top-down: first the big tasks, then break each into subtasks (task 7 → 7.1, 7.2 → 7.2.1…).

At a minimum a WBS must show D-S-D: Duration, Status (open / in progress / complete) and Dependencies (a task that cannot start until another one finishes).

The class example: "implement a new IT training class" (S15–S16):

3Compare vendors22In progress

6Disseminate information25Open
7Create and administer survey (7.1–7.8)46Open
8Analyze results and choose vendor24, 7Open

* Small slide mismatch: the WBS says task 2 depends on 1, but the Gantt chart (S20) and network diagram (S23) start task 2 on day 1 with no predecessor. Use the network diagram for the critical path.

cards.h: Gantt chart: the WBS as bars
cards.body:
A Gantt chart is "a horizontal bar chart that shows the same task information as the project WBS but in a graphical way". It shows the high-level status faster than the WBS.

  • Tasks are rows; time runs across the top (hours or days for a short project, weeks or months for a medium one).
  • Each bar starts and ends exactly when the task starts and ends.
  • Bars are filled in proportionally as work is done.
  • Arrows between bars = dependencies. Upside-down triangles or diamonds = milestones. Names next to bars = people assigned.
  • Keep it to about 20–30 tasks; more → make sub-charts.
  • Tools: a spreadsheet, Visio, SmartDraw, or a PM package (like Jira).

Below is the class example. Red = critical tasks, grey = done, the diamond = the "Budget meeting" milestone. Slide typo: S20 says task 4 ends "3/8/12"; it should be 3/18/12 (3 weeks after 2/26).

cards.body:
The network diagram lays out the tasks as a flowchart. It is "a node-and-arc type of graph that shows time estimates in the nodes and task dependencies on the arcs".

  • Node (box) = one task: name, ID, duration, start and finish dates.
  • Arc (arrow) = a dependency between two tasks.
  • One diagonal line through a node = task partially completed.
  • Crossed lines (an X) = task completed.
  • Critical tasks get a special border (double/thick).

In the class figure: tasks 1, 2 and 11 are crossed (done); 5 and 9 have one diagonal (partly done). The thick boxes below are the critical path.

cards.h: PERT: when you are not sure about the time
cards.body:
Sometimes you really don't know how long a task will take. PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) is used "when the individual task time estimates are fairly uncertain".

Instead of one number, you give three: optimistic (o), most likely (m) and pessimistic (p). Then:

PERT estimate = (o + 4 × m + p) / 6

Example: o = 2, m = 4, p = 12 weeks → (2 + 16 + 12) / 6 = 30 / 6 = 5 weeks. The most likely value counts 4 times; the weights 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.

"CPM can be used with or without PERT": you can put PERT estimates into the network and then find the critical path.

cards.h: CPM: the critical path is the LONGEST path
cards.body:
The critical path is "the longest path from the project inception to completion". Every task on it must finish on time, or the whole project is late. Why the longest? Because the project cannot finish before its slowest chain of tasks.

Method 1, list every path (class example, weeks):

PathSumTotal
1 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8 → 102 + 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 317 ← critical
1 → 9 → 102 + 11 + 316
2 → 3 → 4 → 8 → 106 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 316

So the project takes 17 weeks (Wed 1/1 to Tue 4/29/12). The slide marks tasks 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 with double borders. Task 1 is on the path too, but it is already complete, so it is not marked.

The other paths have 1 week spare (17 − 16). (The textbook word for spare time is "slack" or "float"; it is not on the slides.)

cards.h: Method 2: the forward pass (safest for big networks)
cards.body:
Listing paths gets messy when there are many arrows. The forward pass always works:

  1. Tasks with no predecessor: ES (earliest start) = 0.
  2. EF (earliest finish) = ES + duration.
  3. For a task with predecessors: ES = the biggest EF among its predecessors (you must wait for the slowest one).
  4. Project duration = the biggest EF of all.
  5. Walk back from the end through the predecessor that gave the biggest EF: that is the critical path.

check.q: What three things must a WBS show at a minimum?
check.a: Duration, current status, and task dependencies (D-S-D).

check.q: On a network diagram, what do one diagonal line and crossed lines mean?
check.a: One diagonal line = task partially completed. Crossed lines = task completed.

check.q: On a Gantt chart, how is a milestone shown?
check.a: With an upside-down triangle or a diamond.

check.q: A task has o = 3, m = 5, p = 13 days. What is its PERT estimate?
Is the critical path the shortest or the longest path? Why?
check.a: The longest. The project cannot finish before its longest chain of dependent tasks, so any delay there delays the whole project.

check.q: In the registration example, what happens if E takes 2 weeks longer? If D takes 1 week longer?
check.a: E + 2: its longest path becomes 13, still under 14, so the end date does not change. D + 1: the critical path becomes 15, so the project ends 1 week later.

exam.question: The café ordering app has these tasks (weeks): A Gather requirements 3 (–); B Design screens 2 (A); C Design database 4 (A); D Build front end 5 (B); E Build back end 2 (C); F Integrate and test 2 (D, E); G Train staff 1 (F). Draw the network diagram and the Gantt chart, find the critical path and the total duration, and say which tasks can slip and by how much.

Network: A → B → D → F → G and A → C → E → F (F waits for both D and E).

memorize: Tasks → WBS → Gantt chart + network diagram
WBS minimum: Duration, Status, Dependencies; built top-down, numbered 7 → 7.1 → 7.2.1
Gantt: rows = tasks, time across the top, filled bars = progress, ◆/▼ = milestone, arrows = dependencies, ~20–30 tasks

Forward pass: ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + duration

'Forward pass', 'ES/EF' and 'slack' are textbook terms, not on the slides; on the exam also list the paths (the slide's own method).

label: W4·4
title: Estimating time and keeping the plan honest: trade-offs, workplans, hurricane model, missed dates
hook: After this lesson you can explain the functionality-time-cost trade-off, the 3 problems of WBSs, use the hurricane model's ±100% / ±25% rule, and choose what to do when a schedule date is missed.

cards.h: The three levers: functionality, time, cost
cards.body:
You order a wedding cake. You want it big, tomorrow and cheap. You can usually get only two. Pull one lever and the others move.

The slide: "The science (or art) of project management is in making trade-offs among three important concepts: the functionality of the system, the time to complete the project, and the cost of the project." The manager estimates each lever at the start and then keeps re-assessing.

Estimation = "the process of assigning projected values for time and effort".

Where the numbers come from (S27): projects with similar tasks and technologies, or experienced developers. Keep them conservative. Record the actual time and effort, so the next project uses real data. "Most accurate estimates come from experience."

His review MCQ (W5a-S2): "making ___ of size, time and cost" → Trade-offs.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR
  F([Functionality]) <--> T([Time])
  T <--> C([Cost])
  C <--> F

cards.h: The workplan, and why it must grow step by step
cards.body:
A workplan = "a dynamic schedule that records and keeps track of all the tasks that need to be accomplished over the course of the project" (also: "a dynamic and sequential list of all tasks").

Two ways to build it: modify the plan of an existing or completed project, or derive the tasks from the methodology you use.

Agile / object-oriented projects are iterative and incremental, so the workplan must also be iterative and incremental: tasks and time intervals follow the phases, with different tasks for each workflow. This is called an evolutionary WBS and an iterative workplan (S29).

cards.h: The 3 problems of a traditional WBS (S30–S32)
cards.body:
#ProblemWhy it hurts
1Focused on the design of the system: it "forces the premature decomposition" of the designIf the problem is not well understood, you must fix the architecture before you understand the requirements
2Wrong level of detail: too many levels too early on large projects, too few on small onesThe WBS must be complete at the start for cost and schedule estimates, so estimates are "wildly inaccurate"
3Project-specific, so hard to compare across projectsManagers can't learn from each other: they "reinvent the wheel" and repeat old mistakes

Memory aid: D-D-C = Design focus, Detail level, Comparison.

Weather forecasters see a new storm far away. With little information (but lots of data on old storms) they predict where it will hit. Their forecast "cone" is wide at first and gets narrower as the storm comes closer.

Project estimates work the same way. At the start you can only give broad ranges; they become more specific as the product becomes better defined. This is normal, not bad work.

The numbers (S37): a well-done plan at the end of inception has a 100% margin of error for cost and a 25% margin of error for schedule.

The chart (S38): x-axis = stage when the estimate is made (Inception → Elaboration → Construction → Transition); y-axis = schedule time; circle size = estimated cost. The cones get narrower at each stage.

His question (W5a-S3, Micah): plan says $50,000 and 20 weeks → cost $0 to $100,000 (±50,000), schedule 15 to 25 weeks (±5).
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR
  I["Inception: very wide range"] --> E["Elaboration: narrower"]
  E --> C["Construction: narrower still"]
  C --> T["Transition: almost exact"]

cards.body:
Ahead of schedule: move the next deadlines sooner by the same amount, but do not change the promised completion date.

Behind schedule (you missed a date): 3 possible actions.

If you assume the rest of the project is…ActionRisk
simpler than the late part AND simpler than first believed → you can make up the timeDo not change the scheduleHigh
simpler than the late part, no more complex than first estimated → you can't make up the time, but won't lose moreAdd the total time you are behind to the whole schedule (2 weeks late → all dates +2 weeks). Padded time at the end may absorb it.Moderate
as complex as the late part → the estimates were too optimisticAdd the same percentage to all remaining estimates (2 weeks late on an 8-week part → +25%). If the sponsor can't accept the new date, reduce the scope.Low

Pattern: the more pessimistic your assumption, the lower the risk.

example.problem: A project was planned for 20 weeks. Analysis was planned for 4 weeks but took 5. The remaining work is planned for 16 weeks. What is the new end date under each of the three actions?
example.solution:
• High risk, do not change the schedule: still promise week 20 (you hope to make up 1 week).
  • Moderate risk, add the time you are behind: 20 + 1 = week 21.
  • Low risk, add the same percentage: % behind = weeks late ÷ planned weeks of the late part = 1 ÷ 4 = 25%. Remaining 16 × 1.25 = 20 weeks. New end = 5 + 20 = week 25. If the sponsor can't accept week 25, reduce the scope.

(Checked with python: 1/4 = 0.25; 16 × 1.25 = 20; 5 + 20 = 25.)

check.q: Fill in: "The science (or art) of project management is in making ___ of size, time and cost." (W5a-S2)
check.a: Trade-offs.

check.q: A plan at the end of inception says $80,000 and 12 weeks. What ranges does the hurricane model give?
check.a: Cost ±100%: $0 to $160,000. Schedule ±25%: 9 to 15 weeks.

check.q: Mya (W5a-S3): at the 6-week mark of a 9-week project she is 1 week behind. Best option?
check.a: "About 16% behind, increase the project to about 10.5 weeks": 1/6 ≈ 16.7%, and 9 × 1.167 ≈ 10.5 weeks (the low-risk percentage rule). Adding people or working longer days without changing the schedule are wrong.

check.q: Which action when a date is missed has HIGH risk?
check.a: Do not change the schedule (you assume you can make up the lost time).

check.q: Give the 3 underlying problems of WBSs.
check.a: 1) Focused on the system's design (premature decomposition). 2) Too many or too few levels of detail, so estimates are wildly inaccurate. 3) Project-specific, so hard to compare across projects.

exam.question: (W5a-S3, Micah) A well-done project plan prepared at the end of the planning phase estimates the project at $50,000 and 20 weeks. According to the hurricane model, what is the realistic range?
exam.answer:
The hurricane model says a well-done plan at the end of inception has a 100% margin of error for cost and a 25% margin of error for schedule.

Cost: 50,000 ± 100% × 50,000 = $0 to $100,000.

Schedule: 20 ± 25% × 20 = 20 ± 5 = 15 to 25 weeks.

The ranges narrow as the project moves through elaboration, construction and transition.

memorize: Trade-offs: functionality, time, cost
Estimation = assigning projected values for time and effort
Numbers: similar projects or experienced developers; conservative; record actuals
WBS problems: design focus, wrong detail level, hard to compare
Hurricane: ±100% cost, ±25% schedule (end of inception)
Missed date: no change = high risk; add the weeks = moderate; add the % = low
% behind = weeks late ÷ PLANNED weeks of the late part
note: The 4 stages on the hurricane chart (Inception, Elaboration, Construction, Transition) are not defined on any slide.

label: W4·5
title: Scope creep, timeboxing, risk management and JIRA
hook: After this lesson you can explain scope creep and its causes, list the 5 scope techniques and the 6 timeboxing steps, fill in a risk assessment, and name JIRA's boards and issue types.

cards.h: Scope creep: the #1 reason projects run late
cards.body:
You build the café ordering app. Halfway through, the owner says: "Can we also add a loyalty card? And delivery tracking?" Each wish is small, but together they push the deadline and the budget.

Scope creep = "new requirements are added to the project after the original project scope was defined and frozen". It is "the most common reason for schedule and cost overruns", and it happens after the project is under way.

3 causes (S33):

  1. Users suddenly see the system's potential and want new functions.
  2. Developers discover interesting capabilities and get attached to them.
  3. A senior manager wants the system to support a new strategy from a board meeting.

It has a "deleterious" (harmful) effect on the schedule, and the project manager is responsible for managing changes to reduce it (S45).

1. Identify all requirements at the outset (at the start).
  2. Allow only changes deemed absolutely necessary.
  3. Carefully examine the impact of suggested changes.
  4. Delay some changes as "future enhancements".
  5. Timeboxing.

Café example: the loyalty card is nice but not needed for launch → technique 4, put it in version 2.

Normal projects are task-oriented: more tasks = a longer project. Some companies hate long projects, so they use a time-oriented approach "that places meeting a deadline above delivering functionality". That is timeboxing, "another approach to scope management".

6 steps (S35):

  1. Set the date for system delivery.
  2. Prioritize the functionality to include.
  3. Build the core of the system (the most important functions).
  4. Postpone functionality that cannot be provided in time.
  5. Deliver the system with core functionality.
  6. Repeat steps 3–5 to add refinements and enhancements.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  S1["1. Set the delivery date"] --> S2["2. Prioritize functionality"]
  S2 --> S3["3. Build the core"]
  S3 --> S4["4. Postpone what does not fit"]
  S4 --> S5["5. Deliver with core functionality"]
  S5 -.->|"6. Repeat 3 to 5"| S3

cards.body:
Risk management = "the process of assessing and addressing the risks that are associated with developing a project". The slide calls it the "final facet" of project management.

4 causes of risk (S42): weak personnel, scope creep, poor design, overly optimistic estimates.

6 gears (S43, no order printed): Awareness, Identify, Evaluate, Controls, Implement, Monitor.

Risk assessment template (S44):

FieldClass example
Risk 1The team has never programmed in Java, so development will be slowed
LikelihoodHigh probability
Potential impactProgramming tasks take about 50% longer
Ways to address itUp-front Java training; bring in outside Java experts for early programming

Boards: JIRA supports Scrum and Kanban boards (from W2). A board gives an immediate snapshot of the project, shows progress and each task's status, and its workflow can be customized.

Business project templates: ready templates for simple tasks and complex workflows, customizable per team.

5 issue types (S47):

  • Epic: "a big user story that needs to be broken down".
  • Story: a user story.
  • Task: something that needs to be done to achieve the team's goal.
  • Sub-Task: a smaller piece of an issue.
  • Bug: "a problem that impairs or prevents the functions of the product".

Notice the WBS idea again: big items are broken down into smaller ones.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  EP["Epic: Online ordering"] --> ST1["Story: customer orders a coffee"]
  EP --> ST2["Story: customer pays online"]
  ST1 --> SB1["Sub-task: menu screen"]
  ST1 --> SB2["Sub-task: cart screen"]
  BG["Bug: total price is wrong"] -.-> ST2

example.problem: The café app must launch before Navruz (fixed date). Midway, (1) the owner asks for a loyalty card, (2) a developer wants to add an AR menu "because it is cool", (3) the team has never used Flutter before. Which W4 ideas apply to each?
example.solution:
• (1) and (2) are scope creep: (1) comes from a user/manager seeing new potential, (2) from a developer attached to an interesting capability. Examine the impact; allow only absolutely necessary changes; delay them as future enhancements.
  • The fixed Navruz date → timeboxing: set the date, prioritize, build the core (menu, order, pay), postpone the rest, deliver, then repeat for version 2.
  • (3) is a risk (weak personnel / new technology). Assessment: likelihood high; impact maybe +50% programming time; address it with up-front Flutter training and an outside expert, like the Java example.

check.q: "The most common reason for schedule and cost overruns is ___" (W5a-S2)
check.a: Scope creep.

check.q: Name the 3 sources of scope creep.
check.a: Users who see new potential; developers attached to interesting capabilities; a senior manager adding a new strategy.

check.q: What does step 6 of timeboxing say?
check.a: Repeat steps 3 through 5 (build core, postpone, deliver) to add refinements and enhancements.

check.q: Give the 4 causes of risk on S42.
check.a: Weak personnel, scope creep, poor design, overly optimistic estimates.

check.q: Which JIRA issue type is 'a big user story that needs to be broken down'?
check.a: Epic.

exam.question: What is scope creep? Why does it happen, and what techniques can a project manager use to manage the project scope? Explain timeboxing.
exam.answer:
Scope creep happens when new requirements are added after the project scope was defined and frozen. It occurs after the project is under way and is the most common reason for schedule and cost overruns.

Causes: users see the system's potential and want new functions; developers get attached to interesting capabilities; a senior manager wants the system to support a new strategy.

Techniques: identify all requirements at the outset; allow only absolutely necessary changes; carefully examine the impact of changes; delay some changes as future enhancements; timeboxing.

Timeboxing is a time-oriented approach that puts meeting the deadline above delivering all functionality: 1) set the delivery date; 2) prioritize functionality; 3) build the core; 4) postpone what cannot fit; 5) deliver with core functionality; 6) repeat 3–5 for enhancements.

memorize: Scope creep = new requirements after scope is frozen; #1 cause of overruns
Causes: users, developers, senior manager
5 techniques: identify all at outset, only necessary changes, examine impact, delay as future enhancements, timeboxing
Timeboxing: date → prioritize → core → postpone → deliver → repeat 3–5
Risk causes: weak personnel, scope creep, poor design, optimistic estimates
Risk template: risk, likelihood, impact, ways to address
JIRA: Scrum + Kanban boards; Epic, Story, Task, Sub-Task, Bug
